claim: Neither theory alone explains insight performance: in matchstick algebra, chunk tightness (representational change) and equation value size (progress monitoring) both change solve rates, and they interact (standard tautology 12% at low value vs 62% at high value; reverse tautology 72% vs 77%).
schema_part: trigger: knowledge trigger plus progress trigger (S-stall, O-reframe)
agent_test: Run matchstick-style items with factorial cues (tight vs loose chunk, large vs small distance) on the agent; compare triggers at equal tokens.

claim: Representational change predicted solving better than progress monitoring in Jones 2003 car-park task (normal board 7/13 solved unaided vs rotated 12/13 and easy-practice 12/13; N=39), but the counts are reconstructed from a garbled table in sibling folder 04 and only the abstract was read in this folder.
agent_test: Replicate with an LLM on a Rush Hour style puzzle: change layout framing vs add a distance-to-goal cue; measure solve rate.

claim: A reframing hint alone does not raise solving on a multi-step insight problem; adding an explicit search criterion (maximise intersections) does (ten-penny: control 3/30, line hint 2/29, intersection hint 6/28, maximisation hint 21/29; chi2(1,59)=23.80 verified; N=116 analysed of 120).
schema_part: O-reframe paired with a search criterion
agent_test: Compare reframe-only vs reframe+criterion operator at equal tokens on constrained construction tasks.

claim: Variation of attempts (not repeating one strategy) separates solvers from non-solvers; low variation marks non-solvers (variation rate .59 vs .43; 33% of controls used only the pennies strategy).
agent_test: Log attempt similarity; trigger a forced-different attempt when similarity exceeds a threshold; test vs no trigger.

claim: Working memory span predicts success mainly when the initial search space is large; restructuring itself shows little WM dependence, so search and restructuring are partly separable, but verbal CRA work reads WM as supporting a search account.
agent_test: Vary branching factor of items; check the stall trigger helps more in small-space items than large-space ones.

claim: Staged account: progress monitoring fixes when the search for alternatives begins, representational change fixes how it succeeds (Jones merge proposal, Ollinger 2014 hint groups, Ollinger 2006 factorial where representation had strong effect and heuristics minimal).
agent_test: Ablate: progress trigger only, operators only, both, at equal tokens.

claim: Frame discovery transfers only to the same problem type: after a first success, same-type later accuracy 83.7% vs 44.0%; accuracy rose .32 to .75 over 5 trials in Same vs .32 to .39 in Different (N=189, verified).
agent_test: Test frame memory keyed by problem type vs untagged memory across sequences of matchstick-like items.

claim: The Knoblich 1999 matchstick difficulty order (value changes easiest, tautology hardest) reproduces in Ormerod 2020 and in a large online think-aloud sample (value-loose-chunk 80.7%, tautology 19.2%, N=189, 945 trials, verified).
agent_test: Use the ordered item classes as a difficulty ladder for the agent.

claim: No study found tests an LLM on a Jones-style RCT-vs-progress-monitoring contrast; the closest LLM work (NazoNazo, MathSticks, Illusion of Insight) tests insight-type items without theory-specific predictions.
agent_test: Build the first head-to-head: factorial matchstick or Rush Hour items with theory-specific predictions.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 0 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLMs do far worse than humans on representational-shift riddles: humans 52.9% (n=126), non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6% on the 120-item subset; over all 201 items reasoning vs non-reasoning gives Welch d=0.946 and OR 2.29; parameter size not predictive (r=-0.017). All verified.
agent_test: Run our scaffold vs plain on the same riddle set at equal tokens.

claim: Verification failure: reasoning models often write the correct candidate in the thought log and then do not endorse it (5.23% to 39.34% of incorrect answers by model).
agent_test: Count gold-in-trace-but-rejected rate with and without an explicit endorsement step.

claim: Spontaneous mid-trace Aha shifts in RL-tuned models are rare (6.31% of traces) and go with lower accuracy (2.57% vs 16.44%; Math -19.78pp), so self-generated shifts are not a reliable trigger (verified).
schema_part: trigger design: do not rely on spontaneous Wait
agent_test: Compare spontaneous vs externally gated shift on the same items.

claim: An externally added reconsideration cue after a first answer helps on math (32.21% to 40.62%, +8.41pp, N=320,000, verified) but not on crosswords (+0.45pp) or Rush Hour (+0.01pp); gains are larger when entropy is high. Near-zero gains on crosswords (+0.45pp, base 9.7%) and Rush Hour (+0.01pp, base 0.02%) sit at or near a floor for 1.5B-8B models, so the null is uninformative about gating on puzzles.
agent_test: Gate the second pass by uncertainty; compare with an ungated second pass at equal tokens. Our own forced-doubt note (92% vs 75%) suggests ungated doubt hurts.

claim: LLMs are fixated by red herrings, not fixed by few-shot examples; Einstellung-style mental set also appears and chain-of-thought helps only partly.
agent_test: Test restart with a red-herring-stripped restatement vs continuing.

claim: Matchstick LLM failure is partly perception: o3 60.0% with text vs 38.5% pure visual; humans 91.72% (n=3); reasoning models beat base models by large margins.
agent_test: Use text-form items to isolate restructuring from parsing.

claim: Results on classic verbal insight items conflict across LLM studies: ChatGPT matched typical human scores (12 of 30) and GPT-4 solved 4.5 of 5 items, while BRAINTEASER shows ChatGPT 53-63% vs humans 91.7%; metacognitive prompting above 98% is second-hand only.
agent_test: Prefer novel unpublished items; check public items for memorisation.

claim: Eye tracking shows an abrupt, non-linear attention shift to the key element just before the answer in matchstick problems (34% solved unaided, +11% after hint), but explicit hints give gradual, different dynamics, so a hint is not the same as a self-made restructure.
agent_test: Compare hint-injected reframe vs self-found reframe in trace dynamics.

claim: Progress-monitoring evidence is partly confounded: lookahead is inferred from the same impasse data as the outcome in Jones 2003, and unlimited-move tasks lack a computable move budget, so the criterion is hard to define.
agent_test: Define a surrogate criterion (no new facts in k steps) and test vs a fixed step cap.

claim: Physical interaction with matchstick problems does not reliably raise solve rates; in a three-experiment conceptual replication only one VR cell showed a credible gain (+6pp, about 92%), and movements went with worse results on operator and tautology problems.
schema_part: S-reframe: external manipulation is not a substitute for a constraint-relaxation step
agent_test: Compare an agent that acts more (more tool calls) vs one that restates and relaxes a constraint, at equal tokens, on tautology items.

claim: Insight-like attention shift is abrupt and late (about the 90% bin in matchstick eye tracking); an explicit hint produces a different, immediate shift.
schema_part: trigger design: do not rely on gradual-drift signals
agent_test: Log candidate-set change per step; check whether a change point precedes success.

claim: An executable CSP model needs only a relative criterion (remaining dots / remaining lines) to trigger widening of the representation; it reproduces under 5% solving, fixation and variant difficulty.
schema_part: S-stall: relative stall criterion from the problem statement (remaining gap / remaining moves)
agent_test: Implement the criterion as a stall detector on a constrained search task; compare with a fixed step budget.

claim: Token entropy is not a safe single stall proxy: the entropy-shift link flips sign by domain (OR 2.05 crosswords, 0.58 math).
agent_test: Fit an entropy threshold per task family on a held-out set.

claim: Classic English insight items are contaminated or saturated for current models; hashed fresh items (NazoNazo) show a large human gap and release date, not size, predicts accuracy (Spearman .402, p=.0123).
schema_part: evaluation: use fresh or hashed items for trigger tests
agent_test: Hold out freshly written items to compare trigger arms.

claim: Unstructured multi-agent exploration lowers accuracy on insight-type situation puzzles (47% protocol cost, 53% convergence cost), so convergence rather than divergence is the weak phase.
agent_test: A/B an endorse step after a divergent phase; count tokens.
